title: Pentecost (Acts 2:1–13)
hookLine: wind, tongues of fire, and everyone hears in their own language

lines: A SOUND LIKE A MIGHTY WIND.
TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.
cards: Jerusalem, packed for a feast. Luke says devout Jews from every nation under heaven were staying in the city.
And in one upstairs room, the apostles, Mary, the women, about a hundred and twenty people in all, have been praying together for days, waiting for something they were promised and can't picture.

Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming." It fills the whole house. And there appear "parted tongues as it were of fire," and one rests on each of them.

teach.b: Pentecost is Greek for fiftieth. It was already a Jewish feast, Shavuot, the feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover: a harvest festival, which Jewish tradition also links with the giving of the Law at Sinai.
That's why the city was full. Now the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit, start speaking, and spill out into the street.

teach.h: THE MIRACLE IS IN THE HEARING.
teach.b: Here's the part that's easy to miss: the miracle isn't only in the speaking. It's in the hearing. The crowd is amazed, because, as Luke says, "every man heard them speak in his own tongue."
Visitors from Parthia and Media, Egypt and Rome, Crete and Arabia each hear the wonders of God in the language they grew up with. Early Christian writers noticed an echo.
At the tower of Babel, in Genesis, one language broke into many and people couldn't understand each other. Here, the languages stay many, and everyone understands. Not everybody is impressed.
Some laugh it off: "These men are full of new wine." It's nine in the morning.

teach.h: EVERY MAN HEARD THEM SPEAK IN HIS OWN TONGUE.
teach.b: But this is the day Catholics call the birthday of the Church; the Catechism says the Church was made manifest to the world at Pentecost. The fearful group behind closed doors becomes a people sent out.
On Pentecost Sunday the priest wears red, for the fire, and the Mass has an old hymn that begins, come, Holy Spirit.

how: Catholics celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter; priests wear red, the Mass includes the sequence Veni Sancte Spiritus, and some Catholics pray 'Come, Holy Spirit' through the day.

games.q: you're a visitor from Egypt in the Jerusalem crowd. a group of Galileans is speaking, and you understand every word in your own language. what do you think?
o: both, depending on who you ask.
games.why: Luke says some were amazed and asked what it meant, and others mocked: "these men are full of new wine."

practice: The Hebrew and Greek words for spirit can also mean breath and wind, so breathe in slowly, and out, and notice the air filling you, the way the wind filled the house.
If you pray, you can say the old words the Church says today, slowly, on the breath: Come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, just keep breathing and notice what feels alive in you.

wordCard.voice: Pentecost. The fiftieth day, the Jewish feast of Weeks, when wind and fire came on the disciples and every visitor heard them in their own language. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the fiftieth (day). the Greek name for Shavuot, fifty days after Passover.

carryVoice: Your line: the birthday of the church. The languages stayed many, and everyone understood. Until tomorrow.
